title: Three Feasts Before the LORD, and Justice in the Gates
summary: Moses sets out Israel's three great pilgrim feasts: Passover with the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the spring, the Feast of Weeks at the wheat harvest, and the Feast of Tabernacles after the autumn ingathering. Each is to be kept at the place God will choose, and the last two are marked by joy shared with servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. The chapter then turns to justice, commanding judges in every town who will not show partiality or take bribes, and forbids Asherah poles and sacred pillars beside God's altar.
story: Chapter 15 set Israel's years in a rhythm of seven with the release of debts and servants. Chapter 16 sets the rhythm of each year around three festivals that retell Israel's story: rescue from Egypt, the gift of harvest in the land, and God's care in the wilderness. All three are drawn to the chosen place of chapter 12, so that the whole nation would gather regularly before God. At verse 18 the law code turns from worship to the leadership of the community, beginning a section on judges, kings, priests, and prophets that runs through chapter 18. Justice in the town gate and joy at the sanctuary belong to the same covenant life.
historical:
The three feasts appear also in Exodus 23:14-17, Exodus 34:18-23, and Leviticus 23, and each is tied to the farming year of the southern Levant. Abib, the month of Passover, falls in March or April and was named for the fresh ears of barley; after the exile Jews used the Babylonian name Nisan. The Feast of Weeks came seven weeks later, at the end of the wheat harvest in late spring. The Feast of Tabernacles came in the autumn, after the grapes and olives had been gathered and pressed. The Gezer Calendar, a short Hebrew inscription usually dated to the tenth century BC, lists the months by their farm work in a similar sequence, including ingathering, sowing, barley harvest, the pruning of vines, and summer fruit.

Passover had begun as a household meal in Egypt (Exodus 12). Deuteronomy requires it to be sacrificed only at the chosen place, and 2 Kings 23:21-23 records that King Josiah held a Passover in Jerusalem unlike any since the days of the judges. Scholars debate whether Deuteronomy's law centralized Passover for the first time or restated an older practice (see the hard question). For the book's date more broadly, see the note on Deuteronomy 5.
cultural:
Ancient festivals were times of feasting, travel, and family reunion, and they were often tied to the gods thought to give fertility. Israel's feasts took the same seasons but told a different story: Passover remembered God's rescue, and Tabernacles remembered the wilderness when Israel lived in temporary shelters. The unleavened bread is called “the bread of affliction” (verse 3), a reminder of the haste of the escape from Egypt. Leaven, a bit of old fermented dough used to raise new bread, had to be removed from the house for seven days.

Joy is commanded, and it is not reserved for landowners. Servants, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows are named as guests at the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of Tabernacles. In an ancient village the town gate was the public square, where elders sat to hear cases and settle disputes. Judges who took bribes were a constant problem in the ancient world, and the prophets later condemned them sharply (Amos 5:12; Micah 3:11). The Asherah pole and sacred pillar (verses 21 and 22) were fixtures of Canaanite shrines, and setting one beside the LORD's altar would have blended his worship with theirs.
literary: Verses 1 to 17 form a festival calendar with a regular pattern: each feast is named, dated, located at the place God will choose, and tied to a reason. The phrase about the place the LORD will choose recurs throughout. The calendar ends with a summary (verses 16 and 17) listing the three pilgrim feasts and requiring that no one appear before the LORD empty-handed. Verses 18 to 20 begin a new section on justice, climaxing in verse 20, where the Hebrew repeats the word for justice for emphasis: “Pursue justice, and justice alone.” Verses 21 and 22 return briefly to worship, a reminder that justice and pure worship belong together.

outline.t: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread
Three times a year before the LORD
No Asherah pole or sacred pillar beside the altar

doctrines.note: Passover keeps the memory of the exodus at the center of Israel's year, “so that you may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt” (verse 3). Israel's identity rests on a remembered act of rescue.
The Feasts of Weeks and Tabernacles celebrate the harvest as God's gift, offered in proportion to how he has blessed each family. The rhythm of the agricultural year becomes a rhythm of thanks.

God's rule shapes public life as well as worship. Judges must not show partiality or take bribes, because they administer the justice of the God who shows no partiality (10:17). Justice is the condition of life in the land.

words.note: Pesach, Passover. The name is linked in Exodus 12 with God passing over the houses marked by the lamb's blood. It refers both to the festival and to the lamb sacrificed for it. In this chapter the Passover animal may come from the herd or the flock.

Chag, feast or pilgrim festival. The word often implies a gathering at a sanctuary, sometimes with procession and dance. Three times a year Israel's men were to go up for a chag, and these feasts became the great occasions for pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

Sukkah, booth or temporary shelter. The Feast of Tabernacles, Sukkot, takes its name from the booths Israel lived in during the wilderness years (Leviticus 23:42-43). Observant Jews still build booths for the festival today.

Tsedeq, righteousness or justice. Verse 20 doubles the word, literally justice, justice you shall pursue, a Hebrew way of giving emphasis. Tsedeq means conduct that matches what is right, and for judges it means verdicts that do not bend for wealth, status, or bribes.

christ: Jesus was crucified at Passover, and Matthew, Mark, and Luke present his last supper with his disciples as a Passover meal (John's chronology places the crucifixion as the Passover lambs were being prepared) in which he gave the bread and cup new meaning as his body and blood (Luke 22:14-20). Paul writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,” and urges believers to live as a new unleavened batch (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Holy Spirit was poured out on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:1), the Greek name for the Feast of Weeks, when pilgrims from many nations were in Jerusalem. At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus stood and invited the thirsty to come to him and drink, speaking of the Spirit (John 7:37-39). The New Testament writers saw in these feasts the shape of what God was doing in Christ, while the feasts themselves continue as the heart of Jewish worship.

hard.q: Exodus describes Passover as a meal in each home, but Deuteronomy requires it at the central sanctuary. Why the difference?
hard.a:
In Exodus 12 the first Passover was kept in family homes in Egypt, with blood on each doorpost. Deuteronomy 16 forbids sacrificing the Passover in the towns and requires it at the place God will choose. Many scholars read this as a deliberate change reflecting centralized worship, possibly connected with Josiah's reform, since 2 Kings 23:22 says no Passover like his had been kept since the judges. Those who hold to Mosaic authorship generally see the Exodus account as describing the first, unique Passover in Egypt, and Deuteronomy as giving instructions for its ongoing observance once Israel had a sanctuary in the land, much as Numbers 9 already describes a Passover kept by the whole camp in the wilderness. Some also note that the meal could still be eaten by families, while the sacrifice itself belonged at the sanctuary.

In the time of Jesus, Passover lambs were slaughtered at the Jerusalem temple and eaten by families and groups in homes across the city, combining both elements. After the temple's destruction in AD 70, Jewish Passover returned to the home in the form of the Seder meal, without the sacrifice.

questions: Israel's year was shaped by feasts that retold God's saving acts. What rhythms in your life help you remember what God has done?
The feasts required joy to be shared with servants, foreigners, orphans, and widows. Who might be missing from your own celebrations?
Verse 19 says a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise. What kinds of pressure or reward make it hard for you to see and do what is right?
